title: PESI (Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index)
sources: Aujesky D et al. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2005; ESC 2019 Acute PE guideline

changelog.change: Initial entry — from ED_ICU_OR_Calculators.xlsx. Original (non-simplified) PESI.

purpose: Predicts 30-day mortality after acute PE across five risk classes. Classes I–II identify low-risk patients who may be eligible for outpatient or early-discharge management. The score is the patient's age in years plus the weighted points below.

inputs.label: Altered mental status (disorientation, lethargy, stupor, coma)
O2 saturation < 90% (with or without supplemental O2)

formulas.label: PESI score
formulas.expression: age + male + cancer + hf + lung + pulse110 + sbp100 + rr30 + temp36 + ams + sao2

interpretation.label: Class I (≤ 65) — very low risk, 30-day mortality 0–1.6%. Candidate for outpatient management if nothing else requires admission (see Hestia criteria)
Class II (66–85) — low risk, 30-day mortality 1.7–3.5%. Candidate for early discharge
Class III (86–105) — intermediate risk, 30-day mortality 3.2–7.1%. Admit; assess RV function and troponin
Class IV (106–125) — high risk, 30-day mortality 4.0–11.4%. Admit to a monitored bed
Class V (> 125) — very high risk, 30-day mortality 10.0–24.5%. Monitored / ICU bed; watch for deterioration requiring rescue reperfusion

notes: Classes I–II ≈ sPESI 0. PESI does not by itself indicate thrombolysis — a normotensive PE with RV dysfunction plus a positive troponin is 'intermediate-high' and needs monitoring for haemodynamic decompensation, not upfront lysis. A haemodynamically unstable PE is high-risk regardless of PESI.
buildNote: Formula engine — total = age (years) + weighted select points. Five prognostic classes.
